predecessors.name: Mongol Empire
predecessors.text: China, Mongolia and the east under Kublai's line, with the province of Zhengmian (northern Burma to Tagaung, mongol-empire ledger/86)

successors.name: Ming dynasty
successors.text: the Yuan land the Ming take in 1369: Taiyuan and Shanxi (January 1369), Shaanxi (by September 1369) (Hongwu Emperor page); the Ming ledger dates every later gain itself (Shangdu and the Inner…

successors.name: Northern Yuan
successors.text: the Mongolian Plateau, where the Genghisid court retreated in 1368 (P1)

successors.name: Principality of Liang (Yunnan)
successors.text: Yunnan, where the Prince of Liang Basalawarmi held out until 1381 (P1)

successors.name: Tibet
successors.text: Ü-Tsang, central Tibet, superseded from Sakya rule in 1354-1358 (P4)

ledger.x: 1294: Kublai dies on 18 February and Temür Khan succeeds him; the Yuan stands as the eastern khanate among the four successors of the Mongol Empire.
Goryeo is a Yuan tributary throughout the dossier's first six decades.
Tibet under the Sakya lamas as the Yuan's client government.
1294 (bookkeeping): the fight with Kaidu's House of Ogedei over the Altai and western Mongolia passes from the mongol-empire row to this one; the ogedeid-ulus dossier dates its contest to 1289.
1294 (bookkeeping): the Mongol war with the Sakhalin Ainu passes from the mongol-empire row to this one.
January 1300: Athinkhaya's army 'seized lightly manned southernmost Mongol garrisons' at Singu and Male, about 70 km from Tagaung.
1301: Kaidu dies after the battle near Karakorum and the House of Ogedei's war on the Yuan ends.
4 April 1303: the Mongols 'withdrew from northern Burma entirely on 4 April 1303'.
4 April 1303: the Yuan abolish the province of Zhengmian, evacuate Tagaung and return to Yunnan.
1308: the Northern Sakhalin Ainu are subdued.
1348: Fang Guozhen, accused of piracy, flees to sea and holds the Zhejiang coast outside Yuan control.
September 1351: Zou Pusheng takes Qishui and enthrones Xu Shouhui as emperor of the Tianwan, the first lasting rebel state of the Red Turban Rebellions.
1352: the Tianwan holds the Wuhan cities.
1352-1353: Tianwan forces advance to Jiujiang and take Nanchang and Changsha.
1352: the Wuhan cities leave the Tianwan.
1353: the Yuan army under Toqto'a retakes the Tianwan land.
1353: Zhang Shicheng seizes Gaoyou, the base of his later state.
16 March 1355: Han Lin'er is proclaimed emperor of a restored Song at Bozhou.
1356: Zhang Shide's army takes Changshu (February), Suzhou (March) and pushes west and south into northern Zhejiang.
1356: Ni Wenjun retakes Hanyang and moves the Tianwan capital there.
1356: Tianwan holds Huguang.
1356: King Gongmin's army retakes the northern provinces from the Yuan.
1356: Gongmin cuts the ties with the Yuan.
By 1356 (bridging): Fang holds the Zhejiang ports.
10 April 1356: Zhu Yuanzhang takes Nanjing, the base of the future Ming.
1357: Chen Youliang, who replaced Ni Wenjun in 1357 (P2), holds Jiangxi; P2 says only that he was 'ejected from Jiangxi in 1361'.
1357: Ming Yuzhen takes Sichuan for the Tianwan.
1357: the Song government's Shandong province.
1357 (bridging): Putian.
1357 (bridging): the Yuan side fights the Ispah army for Putian and the approach to Fuzhou.
March 1357: 'Sayf ad-Din and Amir ad-Din, the commanders of the Ispah army, seized the opportunity to control Quanzhou'.
1358: Zhu Yuanzhang holds four inland Zhejiang prefectures.
1358: the Sakya regime's rule over Tibet ends and the tint ends with it.
11 June 1358: the Red Turban Song's Kaifeng campaign begins.
June 1358: Liu Futong's army takes Kaifeng.
1359: Chaghan Temür drives the Song back from Bozhou and Yingzhou to Anfeng.
By 1360: Zhu Yuanzhang holds the south bank of the Yangtze round Nanjing and southern Anhui.
10 September 1359: the Song retreat from Kaifeng.
10 September 1359: the fighting over Kaifeng ends with the Song retreat (P2).
1362: the Song provinces other than Jiangnan are gone.
1363: Zhang Shicheng takes Hangzhou and declares himself Prince of Wu.
1363: northern Jiangsu.
1366: 'it was eventually crushed by the ethnic Han commander Chen Youding' (loyal to the Yuan); the infobox gives a Yuan victory.
1366: Chen Youding crushes the Ispah army and Quanzhou and Putian return to the Yuan.
26 April 1368: the first dated clash between the new Ming and the Yuan army.
By 15 August 1368: Henan is Ming ground.
14 September 1368: Dadu falls and the Yuan court leaves China.
September 1368: the fighting for the North China plain ends with the fall of Dadu.
September 1368: the court retreats to the steppe and continues as the Northern Yuan.
Yunnan holds out for the Yuan.
14 September 1368: the Yuan dynasty ends with the fall of Dadu.

wars.name: Red Turban Rebellions
wars.outcome: The Yuan loses the south to rebel states, and Zhu Yuanzhang, a former Red Turban commander, crushes his rivals one by one (Chen Youliang killed at Poyang Lake in 1363, Zhang Shicheng at Suzhou on 1 October 1367, Fang Guozhen's surrender in 1367) and proclaims…

wars.name: Ming northern campaign of 1368
wars.outcome: Ming victory: Dadu falls on 14 September 1368, Toghon Temür flees to Shangdu (taken 20 July 1369) and then Karakorum, and the Yuan rump continues as the Northern Yuan.

wars.name: War of the Two Capitals
wars.outcome: 'Khanbaliq-based Tugh Temür eventually won the civil war against Ragibagh known as the War of the Two Capitals.'

wars.name: Kaidu-Kublai war, Yuan phase (Yuan and the western khanates)
Mongol campaigns against the Ainu (Mongol invasions of Sakhalin, Yuan phase)
wars.outcome: Mongol victory (infobox 1264-1308): in 1308 the Northern Sakhalin Ainu surrendered and promised a yearly tribute of furs, 'the war between the Ainu and the Mongols was over'.

certainty.note: The steppe, Siberian, Tarim and Tibetan frontiers are approximate; the provincial frontiers of China follow the Branch Secretariats of P1 but no survey line is given; Korea's frontier follows the goryeo dossier's outline.
The front lines between the Yuan and the rebel states moved with each campaign and are drawn by province or by city radius; none is a surveyed line.
